sections.heading: Remembering when I first saw what Christ had done
sections.text: Father, thank you for the day you opened my eyes to see Jesus clearly. In him, your law was honored, your judgment against my sin was answered, death lost its final claim, my guilt was forgiven, and my soul was rescued. I did not create that moment; you gave it to me. Help me never to treat it lightly.
theological_themes: God graciously reveals the saving work of Christ to sinners.
Christ fulfills what we could not fulfill, bears judgment, conquers death, and brings forgiveness.

scripture_references.connection: Paul explains that sinners are justified by God's grace through Christ's redeeming work, where God deals justly with sin while showing mercy to those who believe.
This passage ties salvation to God's purpose and grace in Christ, who has broken the power of death and brought life to light through the gospel.

sections.heading: Trusting your daily faithfulness
sections.text: Since then, you have not left me to myself. Day by day, you have kept proving that the blood of Jesus is enough for me. Day by day, your Spirit has strengthened me, taught me, corrected my steps, and kept changing me from the inside out. I am still needy, but I am not abandoned.
theological_themes: God remains faithful after conversion, applying Christ's work to the believer's life.
The Holy Spirit teaches, leads, strengthens, and sanctifies God's people.

scripture_references.connection: The believer's ongoing access to God rests on the blood of Jesus, giving confidence to draw near with a cleansed conscience.
Jesus promises that the Holy Spirit will teach his disciples and bring his words to their remembrance, grounding the prayer's dependence on the Spirit as teacher and guide.
Paul describes salvation as God's work through the Spirit's sanctifying activity and belief in the truth, fitting the prayer's emphasis on daily inward change.

sections.heading: Refusing every other foundation
sections.text: I do not want to build my life on anything but Christ. I do not need a better hope than the truth of the gospel. I do not need some deeper secret than looking again and again to the cross. Forgive me for the times I have tried to add to what Jesus has already finished. Forgive me when I have quietly leaned on my knowledge, my experiences, my obedience, or my usefulness, as if those things could make me acceptable to you. Even my best works are not clean enough to stand on before you. Let my heart keep saying, “Jesus only. Jesus only.”
theological_themes: Christ alone is the foundation of salvation.
Human knowledge, experience, and works cannot complete or improve Christ's finished work.
Repentance includes renouncing subtle forms of self-righteousness.

scripture_references.connection: Paul states that no foundation can be laid other than Jesus Christ, directly supporting the prayer's refusal to build hope on anything else.
This verse contrasts justification by faith in Christ with reliance on works of the law, grounding the confession that even religious effort cannot make a sinner right with God.
Isaiah's image of polluted garments expresses the inadequacy of even human righteous deeds when considered apart from God's mercy, which fits the prayer's rejection of self-reliance.

sections.heading: Receiving all I have in Jesus
sections.text: In Jesus, I am no longer condemned. In Jesus, I have a righteousness I could never produce. In Jesus, I share in a life that death cannot kill. In Jesus, I am joined to him in a bond that I cannot hold together by my own strength and that he will not break. You have given me more than I can take in. Make my heart larger, so I can receive more of what is already mine in him.
theological_themes: Union with Christ brings freedom from condemnation, righteousness, life, and secure fellowship with him.
The believer asks for greater capacity to grasp and enjoy the fullness already given in Christ.

scripture_references.connection: Paul declares that there is no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus and roots that freedom in God's work through his Son, not in the believer's achievement.
This passage teaches the exchange at the heart of the gospel: Christ bears sin so that believers become the righteousness of God in him.
Jesus describes the believer's life as abiding in him, showing that fruitfulness and spiritual vitality come from union and dependence, not independence.

sections.heading: Running to Christ in failure, temptation, weakness, and despair
sections.text: When I turn away from you, do not let me make peace with my sin. Bring me to honest grief, like Peter, and draw me back to Jesus. When temptation confuses me and I do not know what to do, give me enough strength simply to trust him. When I feel weak, let me collapse into his steady love instead of pretending I am strong. When life presses me to the edge and I see no way out, remind me that he is able to deliver me. And if I feel as though hope itself is gone, give me grace to fall into his arms.
theological_themes: True repentance grieves sin and returns to Christ rather than hiding from him.
In temptation, weakness, extremity, and despair, the believer's refuge is Christ's mercy and power.
God sustains his people when their own wisdom and strength fail.

scripture_references.connection: Peter's bitter weeping after denying Jesus provides the model for sorrow over sin that does not end in hiding, but prepares the way for restoration.
Paul teaches that God remains faithful in temptation and provides a way to endure, supporting the prayer for strength when the believer has no wisdom of his own.
Paul describes being burdened beyond strength so that he would rely not on himself but on God who raises the dead, matching the prayer's movement from extremity to dependence.

sections.heading: Asking you to do more than I can imagine
sections.text: Father, hear me. I am asking for real mercy, real keeping, real faith, and real change. But you know what I need better than I do, and your generosity is greater than my imagination. Do in me and for me more than I know how to ask, more than I can picture, and more than I would dare to expect apart from your grace.
theological_themes: God's power and generosity exceed the believer's prayers and imagination.
Prayer rests in the Father's wisdom, not merely in the believer's ability to ask well.

scripture_references.connection: Paul praises God as the one able to do far more abundantly than all believers ask or think, which directly grounds the final request for God to exceed the prayer itself.
This passage recognizes the believer's weakness in prayer and the Spirit's help, supporting the request that God would answer beyond the limits of the believer's own words and understanding.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses strong substitutionary and propitiatory language, especially 'wrath appeased.' This is biblically grounded but doctrinally debated among Christians, so the adaptation preserves the idea as 'your judgment against my sin was answered' without reducing it to a vague feeling of forgiveness.

The phrase 'filthy rags' can be misunderstood as saying Spirit-enabled obedience has no value at all. The adaptation applies the image specifically to relying on one's works for acceptance before God, which fits the prayer's concern about self-righteousness.
significant_interpretive_choices: 'The life look' was interpreted as the faith-filled gaze toward Christ crucified rather than a one-time emotional experience only; the adaptation keeps both the first awakening to Christ and the ongoing return to the cross.
'If I am tempted, and have no wit' was rendered as being confused and not knowing what to do, preserving the sense of lacking wisdom or resourcefulness under temptation.
'Faint upon his bosom of eternal love' was rendered as collapsing into Christ's steady love, keeping the image of helpless dependence while avoiding archaic sentimental language.
'Indissoluble union in fellowship with him' was interpreted as secure union with Christ that the believer does not create or maintain by personal strength.
